place: A potter's yard by a clay pit near the stream, with a shaded drying shelf and a wood-fired kiln out back.
lines: dig clay from the pit by the stream
wedge it and throw a pot on the wheel
load the kiln and fire it
outcome: The potter digs and wedges clay, rushing the kneading because market is two days off, and shapes a serviceable-looking pot that dries clean in the shade. Days later, fired in the kiln with the rest of the batch, the pot cracks audibly partway through firing as trapped moisture inside an unworked air pocket turns to steam faster than it can escape. The rest of the batch survives untouched; this one pot is a loss, and the potter can only guess afterward which lump of clay held the flaw.

numbers: how much clay is dug, how long digging takes
how thorough the wedging is, whether any air stays trapped
how thin the walls end up, how long shaping takes
how many days it takes to dry evenly
how hot the kiln gets, how long before the crack appears, how much of the batch is lost

latent: whether a pocket of trapped air survived the wedging, unnoticed until the heat found it
state_after: pot: cracked through one wall, unsellable, still cooling in the kiln
potter: aware the wedging was rushed, wary on the next batch
stress: a flaw introduced early and invisible stays latent through every later step until heat forces it out
temptation: a rule that says pots crack in kilns, instead of deriving it from a property any wet inclusion in any fired material would share: trapped moisture, heat, and expansion

place: A smithy at the edge of the village, forge glowing, the smith stepping out and leaving an apprentice to mind the hammering.
lines: hammer the iron bar on the anvil
quench the blade in the water trough
outcome: Left to mind the anvil, the apprentice keeps hammering after the iron bar has cooled past its glow, and it cracks under a blow instead of drawing out. The smith cuts away the cracked end and forge-welds the bar whole again, at the cost of iron and charcoal and half the afternoon. Back at the trough, the apprentice quenches too fast and at an angle, and the blade comes out warped; the smith straightens it cold, which leaves it usable but quietly weaker than a blade forged clean the first time.

numbers: how hot the iron gets, how long heating takes
how far the iron had cooled before striking, how hard the blow lands
how much iron is lost cutting away the cracked end, how long re-welding takes
how much the blade warps
how much bending is needed, how much strength is lost cold-straightening it

latent: how much invisible stress cold-straightening leaves in the metal, not found until the blade is struck hard
state_after: blade: straightened but weakened where it was bent cold
iron bar: shorter than the stock it started as
apprentice: reminded to watch the color of the iron, not the clock
stress: two independent honest mistakes in one work session compound: wrong heat when struck, then wrong cooling when quenched
temptation: a special rule for 'iron cracks when hammered cold' and another for 'blades warp in water', instead of one property for working temperature and one for differential cooling that any worked metal would share

place: The tanning yard behind the settlement, hides pegged out or piled, a hot spell settling over the village.
lines: set it aside to salt later
outcome: The tanner scrapes a hide clean of fat and flesh, then sets it aside meaning to salt it that evening, but the evening's work runs long and it waits two warm days instead. In that time, with no salt and no smoke to stop it, the hide slips its hair and turns, ruining what would otherwise have been a season's worth of good leather. The tanner only learns how far gone it is when they finally come back for it.

numbers: how long scraping takes, how clean it comes
how many days pass before salting, how warm the weather is
how many days of warmth before the hide turns, how much of it is ruined
how much of the season's hides are lost with it

latent: nobody checks the hide each day, so how far the rot has gone is only found when the tanner comes back for it
state_after: hide: rotten, hair slipping, fit only for the midden
tanner: down one hide for the season's leather
stress: a process left half-finished fails on its own timeline, not the player's
temptation: a rule that hides rot after exactly so many days, instead of deriving spoilage from warmth, moisture and the absence of salt or smoke, the same properties that would spoil meat or fish

place: The brewhouse, a mash tun kept near the hearth for warmth, midsummer.
lines: mash the grain and set the wort by the hearth to ferment
outcome: The brewer mashes malted grain into a sweet wort and sets it by the hearth where it's warm enough to ferment quickly. The same warmth that wakes the yeast also favors the souring bacteria that live on the air and the barrel staves, and over several warm days they outrun the yeast. By the time the brewer tastes it, the batch has turned sour rather than fermented clean, fit for vinegar rather than drinking.

numbers: how much wort comes from how much grain, how long mashing takes
how warm the hearth-side is, how fast fermentation runs
how many days of warmth before souring bacteria outrun the yeast, how much of the batch turns

effects: brewer learns the batch has turned
numbers: how much of the batch can still be used as vinegar rather than poured out

latent: whether the wort was kept too near the hearth is only known once it's tasted
state_after: barrel: full of sour wort, fit for vinegar not drinking
brewer: setting the next batch further from the fire
stress: the same warmth that helps yeast work also helps the bacteria that ruin it; there is no safe setting, only a balance
temptation: a rule naming 'ale' and 'vinegar' as two fixed recipes, instead of one souring process that any sugary, warm, exposed liquid can undergo

place: The village oven, a cold morning before market day.
lines: mix the dough and set it to rise by the oven
stoke the oven hotter, we're behind
outcome: The baker mixes dough and sets it to rise, but the cold morning keeps the yeast sluggish and it rises slower than usual. Behind schedule for market, the baker stokes the oven hotter to make up the time, and the loaves come out with a burnt crust while the underrisen center stays dense and half-raw. Fixing the slow rise by pushing the oven only trades one honest problem for a worse one.

numbers: how much flour and water go in, how long mixing takes
how long the dough takes to rise in the cold, how much less it rises than usual
how much hotter the oven is stoked, how much extra wood it takes
how long baking takes, how much of the loaf is spoiled by burnt crust versus raw dough

latent: how much the cold slowed the dough is only apparent once it comes out of the oven
state_after: loaves: burnt crust, dense raw crumb inside, edible but poor
baker: short of good loaves for market
stress: fixing one problem by pushing a different lever creates a second, worse problem
temptation: a rule tying bread quality to a clock, instead of deriving rise from temperature and time, and baking from heat, moisture and time together

place: A cottage in winter, a spindle by the fire and a loom set up against the wall.
lines: weave the wool on the loom
outcome: Over the winter a child apprentice spins wool into thread by the fire, the twist uneven and thin in patches from an unsteady hand. The weaver dresses the loom with it and weaves cloth for days without trouble, until the warp reaches the thin patch and it snaps under the tension of the beat. The weaver has to pick out the break, re-tie the thread, and carry on, leaving a flaw in the cloth where the weakness finally showed.

numbers: how even the twist is, how thin the thin spots run
how many threads go into the warp, how long dressing the loom takes
how much cloth is woven before the flaw is reached

effects: weaver learns the thread was weak here
numbers: how much weaving time is lost re-tying the broken thread, how visible the flaw is in the finished cloth

latent: which thread in the warp was the thin one is not known until it gives way
state_after: cloth: a re-tied flaw partway across, weaker there than the rest
child apprentice: still learning an even twist
stress: a small unevenness from an early, unrelated process only becomes a problem much later, under a load the first process never saw
temptation: a special case for 'children spin badly', instead of deriving thread strength from the evenness of the twist and cloth flaws from tension meeting a weak point in the material

place: A timber-framed house raised at the edge of the settlement in late spring, built from timber felled that same season.
lines: raise the frame and peg the joints
outcome: In a hurry to close the house up before winter, the carpenter fells an oak, hews it, and raises the frame while the timber is still green, pegging the joints tight. Over the following months the timber dries and shrinks across the grain as any green wood does, and the once-tight joints work loose; the lintel starts to sag under its own weight. Nobody touches the frame in that time; the wood does it to itself.

numbers: how much timber one tree yields, how long felling and hewing takes
how tightly the joints are cut, how long raising the frame takes
how many months seasoning takes, how much the timber shrinks across the grain
how much give appears in the joint, how far the lintel sags

latent: how much the frame will move only shows once a season has passed
state_after: frame: joints loosened, lintel sagging slightly, still standing
carpenter: planning to re-wedge the joints before the first snow
stress: building with unseasoned material trades a fast start for a debt paid later, by the material itself, with nobody touching it
temptation: a rule that houses need repair after one year, instead of deriving shrinkage from moisture loss in wood over time, the same process that dries anything green

place: A wattle panel freshly built onto a house wall, daubed during a hot, dry week.
lines: mix mud and straw and daub the wattle panel
outcome: In a hurry, the dauber mixes mud with less straw than usual and daubs it thickly onto the wattle panel. The hot week dries the coat fast, and with too little straw to bind it as it shrinks, the daub cracks and falls away in patches within days. The dauber mixes a second batch with more straw and recoats the bare wattle, this time measuring rather than guessing.

numbers: how much straw goes in for how much mud, how long mixing takes
how thick the coat goes on, how long applying it takes
how many days of heat it takes to dry, how wide the cracks open, how much of the coat falls away
how much extra mud and straw the second coat costs

latent: how much straw is really needed is only found by how the first coat cracks
state_after: wall: patched with a second, better-mixed coat over the cracked first one
dauber: now measuring the straw instead of guessing
stress: too little binder in a material that must shrink as it dries fails from the inside, not from any outside force
temptation: a rule that walls need redaubing every so often, instead of deriving cracking from a mix's binder content meeting a fast drying rate, the same balance that undermixed mortar would show

place: A cottage roof, rethatched thin and fast before the rains, on a poor year for reed.
lines: thatch the roof with what reed we have this year
outcome: Short on reed, the thatcher lays a thinner coat than usual to get the roof covered before the autumn rains. All winter the rain slowly seeps through the thin patches, and the rafter beneath, kept damp for months, quietly rots without anyone seeing it. The rot only shows itself when a heavy snowfall's weight is more than the weakened rafter can bear, and it gives way, opening a hole in the roof from a shortcut taken in a different season entirely.

numbers: how thick the thatch goes on compared to a full year's coat, how long thatching takes
how many weeks of rain before water reaches the timber beneath
how many months of damp before the rafter weakens, how much strength it loses
how much weight the rafter can no longer bear, how large the hole in the roof ends up

latent: the rot inside the rafter is not seen until the roof itself gives visible sign of it
state_after: roof: sagging with a hole where the rafter gave way
thatcher: due to rethatch properly and the carpenter to replace the rafter
stress: a shortcut taken in one season pays out as structural failure in a different season, through wood and water, not through the thatch itself
temptation: a rule that thin roofs leak after one winter, instead of deriving leaking from thatch depth, rot from wood meeting sustained damp, and collapse from load meeting weakened wood

place: A row of close-built thatched houses next to the smithy, a dry, windy afternoon after weeks with no rain.
outcome: The forge's bellows send sparks up on an ordinary afternoon, and the wind carries one onto a neighboring roof gone tinder-dry after a rainless spell. Because the houses stand close together and the thatch everywhere is just as dry, the fire jumps from roof to roof faster than anyone expects before the villagers can organize. A bucket chain from the well finally beats it back, but not before two roofs burn through and the rest of the row is scorched.

numbers: how far the sparks travel on the wind
how dry the thatch is after the rainless spell, how likely a spark catches

effects: villagers learn the row is on fire
numbers: how many roofs catch before it's stopped, how fast the wind pushes it along the row
how many buckets it takes, how much of the row burns before it's out

state_after: row of houses: two roofs burned through, rest scorched but standing
well: drawn low from the bucket chain
villagers: exhausted, watching for a second flare-up overnight
stress: a hazard nobody built into any one thing only becomes a disaster when dry weather, closeness of houses, and a working forge meet at once
temptation: a rule that thatched rows near forges burn down, instead of deriving ignition from dryness meeting heat, and spread from flammable material meeting wind and closeness

place: The animal pen behind the granary, a fence rail gone soft with rot, harvest just stored for winter.
outcome: A goat leaning against a fence rail that has quietly rotted under an old coat of whitewash finds it gives way, and pushes through the gap into the granary. It eats and tramples part of the grain sacked for winter before a villager notices the gap and pens it back up. Nobody meant for the rail to fail, but the rot was there all along, waiting for enough weight to find it.

numbers: how much weight the rail can take before it gives
how wide the gap ends up
how much grain is eaten versus trampled and spoiled
how much of the winter's grain is now missing

latent: the fence rail's rot was hidden under a coat of old whitewash
state_after: grain sacks: torn open, part eaten, part spilled on the ground
fence: gapped, needs a new rail before anything else gets back in
goat: closed back in the pen
stress: a maintenance failure nobody was watching turns into a resource loss nobody intended
temptation: a rule that goats eat grain if a fence is broken, instead of deriving the breach from a rail's strength meeting an animal's weight, and the eating from any hungry animal meeting reachable food

place: The grain bin in the undercroft, filled in a rushed harvest ahead of early rain.
lines: harvest the field quickly before the rain and sack the grain
outcome: Racing the weather, the farmer brings in the grain and sacks it while it's still a little damp, sealing the bin before it has properly dried. Packed close and shut in, the damp grain generates its own heat over the following weeks, and mold takes hold at the center of the bin with no outside cause at all. Nobody learns how much is spoiled until the bin is opened partway through winter, when good grain on top gives way to a caked, ruined mass beneath.

numbers: how much is brought in before the rain, how damp it still is
how much moisture is left in the grain when it's sacked
how many weeks of sealed damp it takes before the grain heats itself, how much of the bin is affected

effects: farmer learns part of the bin has spoiled
numbers: how much of the stored grain is still good come the opening

latent: whether the grain went in damp enough to spoil itself is not known until the bin is opened months later
state_after: grain bin: good grain on top, a moldy, caked mass at the damp center
farmer: short for the rest of winter, rationing what's left
stress: grain, packed close and sealed, generates its own heat from the same dampness that would rot an open hide, with no outside cause at all
temptation: a rule that grain spoils after a fixed number of months in storage, instead of deriving self-heating from moisture and density, the same property that would spoil hay or compost

place: The village well, its rope replaced once already this year after fraying.
lines: draw a bucket of water from the well
outcome: A villager hauls up a full bucket the way they have hundreds of times this year, on a rope that was spliced once already after fraying against the well's stone lip. The spliced spot was never the true weak point; a different stretch, worn thin from the same rubbing over months, finally parts under the weight and drops the bucket down the shaft. Fishing it back out with a hook and pole takes a while, and the villager learns the rope needs full replacing, not another splice.

numbers: how many times the rope has been hauled this year, how thin the worn spot has gotten
how many hauls it takes to wear through a given number of strands
how far the bucket falls, how likely it is to be fished back out

effects: villager learns a new rope is needed
numbers: how long fishing it out takes, how many tries it takes

latent: exactly where along its length the rope was worn thinnest is not known until it parts there
state_after: rope: parted, both ends still tied off, needs full replacement not another splice
bucket: recovered, dented
well: out of service until a new rope is spun and fitted
stress: a mend that restores use does not restore strength; the weak point keeps being the weak point
temptation: a rule that ropes snap after being spliced once, instead of deriving failure from cumulative wear at a point of friction, the same wear that dulls a blade's edge or thins a hinge

place: A one-room cottage in a cold, wet week, several people and a goat sharing the yard and a single water source.
outcome: A run-down member of the household catches a fever in the cold, damp week, and it passes to the rest through the unwashed cup they all drink from, one or two falling sick a day apart. Too weak to keep up the chores, the household misses several milkings, and the goat goes uncomfortable and short of relief until a neighbor, still well, steps in to milk it for them. The sickness costs the household in an animal's discomfort as much as in their own fever, simply because the household and the goat both depend on the same hands.

numbers: how many days before the fever breaks or worsens

effects: household learns the sickness is spreading
numbers: how many of the household fall sick, how many days apart
how many milkings are missed, how much milk is lost

effects: transfers care from household to neighbor
numbers: how many days the neighbor covers the milking

latent: who in the household will catch it next is not known until they do
state_after: household: two still feverish, one recovering
goat: milked again, thanks to the neighbor
neighbor: owed a favor, by nobody's ledger but memory
stress: sickness moves through a household by the same closeness and sharing that makes a household work at all, and its cost shows up sideways, in an animal, not in the sick
temptation: a rule naming which specific person catches a cold from which other specific person, instead of deriving spread from closeness, contact and a weakened state that would carry any sickness

place: The rutted road into the market square, a cart loaded with a season's fired pots, its axle original to the cart and years old.
lines: load the pots on the cart and drive to market
outcome: The potter loads a season's worth of fired pots onto the cart and sets off down the rutted road to market, on an axle that has carried loads without complaint for years. Worn thinner than anyone thought to check, the axle finally cracks when the cart hits a deep rut, and the cart tips hard enough to spill the load. Several pots smash outright on the road; the rest scatter but survive, and the potter is left short for market and needing the axle mended before the next trip.

numbers: how many pots the cart carries, how heavy the load is
how many years the axle has carried loads, how rough the road is
how sudden the break is, how far the cart tips
how many pots survive the fall, how many are smashed outright

latent: how worn the axle had become was never checked before this trip
state_after: cart: tipped, axle broken, blocking half the road
pots: several smashed, the rest scattered but whole
potter: short for market, needing the axle mended before the next trip
stress: a part that has quietly done its job for years fails on an ordinary day, under an ordinary load, at the worst possible moment
temptation: a rule that carts break down on the way to market, instead of deriving failure from years of accumulated wear meeting one more load on rough ground, the same wear that would fail a rope, a hinge or a handle
